title: ELIZA, the 1966 therapist made of rules
summary: In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA imitated a therapist with keyword rules and no understanding. He was startled by how fast people treated it as human.

beats.say: A program from nineteen sixty six imitated a therapist using simple rules.
Joseph Weizenbaum built it at M.I.T. and named it ELIZA.
Its best known script, DOCTOR, played a therapist who mirrors the patient.
It scanned each sentence for keywords, and every keyword had a priority.
Then it swapped first and second person, so my became your.
beats.cap: Rule at work: my becomes your

beats.say: The first matching rule supplied a reply, and replies took turns.
It understood nothing, and its author said so.
Weizenbaum was startled how quickly people treated it as human.
beats.cap: People treated it as human, fast

beats.say: He opposed using programs like it to treat real patients.
beats.cap: He opposed it as real therapy

beats.say: Pattern matching sounded like care. It was still pattern matching.

facts.claim: Joseph Weizenbaum developed ELIZA at MIT and published about it in 1966
facts.note: Wikipedia, ELIZA: developed at MIT by Joseph Weizenbaum (1964 to 1967); his paper appeared in 1966

facts.claim: Weizenbaum named the program after Eliza Doolittle in Shaw's Pygmalion
facts.note: Harvey, Computer Science Logo Style v2 ch.9: named ELIZA after Eliza Doolittle in Pygmalion

facts.claim: The DOCTOR script imitated a Rogerian psychotherapist by reflecting the patient's statements back
facts.note: Wikipedia, ELIZA: best-known script DOCTOR imitates a Rogerian psychotherapist, mirroring the patient

facts.claim: ELIZA looked for keywords, each with a priority, and used the highest-priority one
facts.note: Harvey: input is split into sentences and searched for keywords, each with a priority; the highest is used

facts.claim: The rules swapped first and second person, for example my to your
facts.note: Harvey: translations swap my/your and I/you so the reflected statement reads correctly; example 'My spirits are low' -> 'Your spirits are low?'

facts.claim: The first matching pattern supplied the reply and replies rotated so the same one did not repeat at once
facts.note: Harvey: the first matching pattern is used; responses rotate so the same reply does not repeat right away

facts.claim: Weizenbaum wrote in 1976 that he was startled by how quickly and unequivocally people anthropomorphized the program
facts.note: ELIZA archaeology page, citing Computer Power and Human Reason (1976, pp. 6-7)

facts.claim: Weizenbaum strongly opposed using programs like ELIZA to give therapy to real patients, and said the program does not understand conversation
facts.note: Harvey: the program does not understand conversation (pattern matching and substitution); Weizenbaum strongly opposed using such programs as therapy for real patients
